title: 2. Tense Mastery & Time Precision (1/2)
group: Module 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine
blocks: The twelve tenses mapped, the five that IELTS rewards, and the two critical pairs (past simple vs present perfect, present simple vs present continuous) that cause almost all tense errors.

Subject-verb agreement made your verbs match. Tense makes them sit in the right time. In IELTS this is not a small point of grammar; it is a matter of meaning. Writing Task 1 describes data that already happened or is happening now, Task 2 predicts and generalises, and Speaking moves constantly between past stories and future plans. Put a verb in the wrong time and you have not just made a grammar slip, you have said something untrue about when it happened. That is why examiners treat tense control as a core signal of the Band 6-to-7 jump.
2.1 What a tense actually is (zero assumption)
An English tense carries two pieces of information at once:
Time: past, present, or future. (When did it happen?)
Aspect: simple, continuous, perfect, or perfect continuous. (Is it a whole finished event, an action in progress, an action linked to another time, or a mix?)

Three times multiplied by four aspects gives the twelve tenses. That sounds like a lot, but the good news for IELTS is that five of them do about 90 per cent of the work, and this chapter foregrounds those five while still showing you the full map so nothing is a mystery.
The four aspects, in plain words:
a whole event, a fact, a habit
an action linked to a later time; “before now / before then”
an action in progress up to a point, with duration
2.2 The complete map of the twelve tenses
Study the whole table once so you can recognise every form. Then move to 2.3, where we foreground the five that matter most.
past action still relevant; trend up to now
duration of an action continuing to now
Prices have been rising for a decade.
finished event at a finished time
action in progress at a past moment
Sales were falling when the law changed.
an earlier past action before another past action
duration up to a point in the past
It had been raining for hours before it stopped.
Demand will rise over the next decade.
action in progress at a future moment
By 2030, most cars will be running on electricity.
an action completed before a future point
By 2040, the city will have doubled in size.
duration up to a future point
By June she will have been working here for ten years.

p.p. = past participle (the third form: go / went / gone; rise / rose / risen). The high-frequency irregular list is in Appendix A at the back of the book. Learn it as fixed items, the way you learned vocabulary.
2.3 The five tenses IELTS actually rewards
You can describe any graph and answer any Speaking question accurately with these five. Master them before you worry about the rest.
Present simple for facts, habits, general truths, and Task 2 positions.
Present continuous for what is happening now and for current trends.
Past simple for finished events and historical graph data.
Present perfect for actions and trends that reach up to the present.
Future (will / going to) for predictions and plans.
Two pairs inside this five cause almost all tense errors. The rest of the chapter drills those two pairs, because fixing them fixes most of your tense marks.

title: 2. Tense Mastery & Time Precision (2/2)
group: Module 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine
blocks: 2.4 Critical pair 1 · Past simple versus present perfect
This is the single most common tense confusion for Bangladeshi candidates, and it is decisive in Task 1.
Use the past simple when the time is finished, and often stated: in 2010, last year, two decades ago, between 2000 and 2010.
Use the present perfect when the action reaches up to now, or when the exact time does not matter: signalled by since, for, over the past decade, recently, so far, already.
Past simple: The population rose in 2010. (a finished year) / Present perfect: The population has risen since 2010. (2010 up to the present)
The clearest signal is the time word:
Signals PRESENT PERFECT (time up to now)
so far, up to now, already, lately
The company has launched its first product in 2009.
The company launched its first product in 2009.
Since 2020, remote work became far more common.
Since 2020, remote work has become far more common.

In Bangla, “আমি দেখেছিলাম” and “আমি দেখেছি” can sound almost the same, so let the time words decide: a specific finished time (in 2010, last year, ago) takes the past simple; since, for or recently takes the present perfect.

Data tied to a past year is past simple; a trend running to the present is present perfect.

Skills: Writing
Task 1: Sales fell in 2015 but have recovered every year since.
2.5 Critical pair 2 · Present simple versus present continuous
Use the present simple for a permanent fact, a habit, or a general truth. This is the tense of most Task 2 topic sentences and of process descriptions.
Use the present continuous for something happening right now or a temporary current trend, especially with words such as currently, at the moment, these days, nowadays.
Present simple (general truth): Governments spend public money on healthcare. / Present continuous (current trend): The number of remote workers is increasing steadily.
Task 2 general truth: Many people believe that university education should be free. / Task 1 current trend: Demand for electric vehicles is rising sharply at present.
2.6 Future forms · will, going to, and the present continuous
Three forms cover the future in IELTS:
will + base verb: predictions, general future facts, and decisions made at the moment of speaking. If this trend continues, sea levels will rise further.
be going to + base verb: plans already decided, and predictions based on present evidence. The government is going to introduce a carbon tax next year.
present continuous: fixed personal arrangements (mostly Speaking). I am meeting my supervisor tomorrow.
For Task 1 projections (a graph that forecasts into the future) and Task 2 consequences, will is the workhorse: Unless emissions are cut, the planet will face irreversible damage.
2.7 The perfect and continuous tenses you should at least recognise
You will not need all twelve constantly, but recognising them lets you read a prompt correctly and adds range when it is natural.
Past perfect (had + p.p.) shows which of two past events came first. Useful in Speaking Part 2 narratives. By the time the report was published, the situation had already changed.
Present perfect continuous (have been + -ing) stresses the duration of a trend reaching now. House prices have been rising steadily for over a decade.
Future perfect (will have + p.p.) projects a completed change by a future point, strong in Task 1 forecasts. By 2040, the population will have doubled.
Use these for genuine range, not decoration. One accurate past perfect in a Speaking narrative shows control; a forced one that does not fit reads as an error.
Two continuous-tense errors dominate Bangladeshi scripts. Both come from over-using the -ing form, partly because Bangla uses its continuous form more freely than English does.

Error type 1 · Stative verbs cannot be continuous. Some verbs describe a state, not an action in progress: know, believe, understand, mean, agree, want, need, prefer, like, love, hate, seem, appear, belong, own, contain, consist, depend, and have when it means possession.
✗ I am knowing the answer. / He is having two cars. / I am understanding your point now.
✓ I know the answer. / He has two cars. / I understand your point now.

Error type 2 · “Since” and “for” take the perfect, not the present continuous. A trend that started in the past and continues now uses the present perfect or present perfect continuous, never the plain present continuous.
✗ The population is increasing since 2010. / Prices are rising for the last five years.
✓ The population has increased / has been increasing since 2010. / Prices have been rising for the last five years.
Time frames win or lose Task 1

In Writing Task 1, tense is not optional accuracy; it is the backbone of the answer. A chart with a past date range must stay in the past simple throughout. A trend that reaches the present takes the present perfect. A graph with a future projection takes will or is expected to. In Task 2, general truths and your own position sit in the present simple, while consequences and predictions take the future.

Skills: Writing, Speaking
Task 1: Car sales peaked in 2015, have fallen every year since, and are expected to stabilise after 2025.
Task 2: Because cities continue to expand, housing shortages will worsen unless governments act now.
Speaking Part 3: Attitudes have changed a great deal recently, and I think they will keep changing.
End of Chapter 2. Chapter 3 (Articles & Noun Types) follows.

title: 2. Practice · Tense Mastery & Time Precision
group: Module 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine
blocks: Of the twelve English tenses, only five do almost all the work in IELTS: present simple, present continuous, past simple, present perfect, and future forms. Master these five before worrying about the rest.
**Why it matters:** You can describe any graph and answer almost any Speaking question accurately with just five tenses.
**Present simple** -- facts, habits, general truths, Task 2 positions.
**Present continuous** -- what's happening now, current trends.
**Past simple** -- finished events, historical graph data.
**Present perfect** -- actions or trends that reach up to now.

Two pairs inside this five cause almost all tense errors in Bangladeshi candidates' writing -- past simple vs present perfect, and present simple vs present continuous. Fixing those two pairs fixes most of your tense marks.

blocks.title: Exercise 2.1 · Tense Selection
blocks.instructions: Put the verb in brackets into the correct tense. Each item has one best answer determined by its time signal or meaning.

items.prompt: In 2008, the company (open) ______ its first overseas office.
items.reason: Finished year (2008), past simple.

items.prompt: Since 2015, the government (invest) ______ heavily in renewable energy.
items.reason: “Since 2015” reaches to now, present perfect.

items.prompt: At the moment, the number of tourists (rise) ______ rapidly.
items.reason: “At the moment”, present continuous.

items.prompt: Water (freeze) ______ at zero degrees Celsius.
items.reason: General scientific truth, present simple.

items.prompt: By the time the survey ended, attitudes (already / change) ______.
items.reason: An action completed before another past event, past perfect.

items.prompt: I (know) ______ the answer to that question. (correct the tense if wrong)
items.reason: “I am knowing” is wrong; know is stative and stays simple present.

items.prompt: House prices (increase) ______ steadily for the last ten years.
items.reason: “For the last ten years” reaches to now; present perfect continuous stresses the duration.

items.prompt: If this trend continues, the population (double) ______ by 2050.
items.reason: A real future prediction, first-conditional future with “will.”

items.prompt: Last summer, the temperature (rise) ______ by three degrees.
items.reason: “Last summer” is finished time, past simple.

items.prompt: Nowadays, more and more people (work) ______ from home.
items.reason: “Nowadays” plus a current trend, present continuous.

items.prompt: The factory (close) ______ down in 1998 and has never reopened.
items.reason: A finished event (1998), past simple.

items.prompt: Over the past decade, technology (transform) ______ the way we communicate.
items.reason: “Over the past decade” reaches to now, present perfect.

items.prompt: He (have) ______ two brothers and one sister. (state, not action)
items.reason: Possession is stative; “is having” would be wrong here.

items.prompt: Between 2000 and 2010, unemployment (fall) ______ gradually.
items.reason: A finished past range (2000 to 2010), past simple.

items.prompt: Currently, the government (consider) ______ three new proposals.
items.reason: “Currently”, present continuous.

items.prompt: She (understand) ______ the problem now, after the explanation. (correct the tense if wrong)
items.reason: “Is understanding” is wrong; understand is stative, present simple.

items.prompt: By 2030, most new cars (be) ______ electric, experts predict.
items.reason: A future prediction for a future point, future simple.

items.prompt: The graph shows that consumption (drop) ______ sharply in 2012.
items.reason: Tied to a finished year (2012), past simple.

items.prompt: So far this year, exports (grow) ______ by twelve per cent.
items.reason: “So far this year” reaches to now, present perfect.

items.prompt: Governments (spend) ______ large sums on defence every year. (general truth)
items.reason: A repeated general truth (“every year”), present simple.

blocks: Past simple or present perfect? It's the single most common tense confusion in Task 1 writing. The rule is about time: finished periods take past simple, periods reaching up to now take present perfect.
**Why it matters:** This is the single most common tense confusion for Bangladeshi candidates, and it's decisive in Task 1 trend description.
Use **past simple** when the time is finished and often stated: in 2010, last year, two decades ago.
Use **present perfect** when the action reaches up to now, or the exact time doesn't matter: since, for, over the past decade, recently.
The population rose in 2010 (a finished year) vs the population has risen since 2010 (2010 up to the present).

Time words like "in 2015" or "two decades ago" call for past simple; "since 2015", "for five years", or "so far" call for present perfect. Train yourself to scan the time expression first -- it tells you the tense before you even think about the verb.

blocks.title: Exercise 2.2 · Task 1 Trend Description
blocks.instructions: Write one paragraph describing the trend, using the past simple for finished data, the present perfect for the change up to the present, and a future form for the projection. Then compare with the model.

items.prompt: Write one accurate paragraph describing the trend for “Coffee consumption per person in Country X, 1990 to 2030 (projected).” Use the past simple for finished data, the present perfect for the change up to the present (assume “now” is 2025), and a future form for the projection. Notes: 1990 low, about 2 kg; rose steadily through the 1990s; 2000 reached 5 kg; fell slightly between 2005 and 2010; has risen again every year since 2010; 2025 stands at about 8 kg; projected to reach 10 kg by 2030.
items.answer: In 1990, coffee consumption in Country X was low, at roughly 2 kilograms per person. It then rose steadily throughout the 1990s, reaching 5 kilograms by 2000. Consumption fell slightly between 2005 and 2010, but it has risen every year since, and it now stands at about 8 kilograms per person. Looking ahead, the figure is projected to reach 10 kilograms by 2030.
accepted: In 1990, coffee consumption in Country X was low, at roughly 2 kilograms per person. It then rose steadily throughout the 1990s, reaching 5 kilograms by 2000. Consumption fell slightly between 2005 and 2010, but it has risen every year since, and it now stands at about 8 kilograms per person. Looking ahead, the figure is projected to reach 10 kilograms by 2030.
items.reason: was, rose, reaching, fell = finished past data with stated years (past simple). has risen = the change reaches the present (present perfect). now stands = the present situation in 2025 (present simple). is projected to reach = a future forecast.
